message.content:
The total number of distinct positions that can arise in a legal game of chess is astronomically large—on the order of **10⁴³**.  

This figure is an estimate based on combinatorial analysis of the board’s 64 squares, the 12 piece types (six for each side), and the rules that restrict how pieces can move and capture.  It is often called the “Shannon number” for positions, after Claude Shannon who first estimated it in 1950.

For comparison, the number of distinct legal games (i.e., sequences of moves from the starting position to any end position) is even larger—roughly **10¹²⁰**.  Both numbers are far beyond the total number of atoms in the observable universe, illustrating why exhaustive search of all possible chess positions is infeasible.
